courses.title: Python Fundamentals
courses.description: Learn to describe small problems with variables, decisions, loops, and reusable Python functions.

lessons.title: Names and Values
lessons.content:
Explanation: A variable name refers to a value. Choose names that describe the value's purpose, and assign a new value when that purpose changes.

Example: learner_name = 'Mira'
completed_lessons = 2
completed_lessons = completed_lessons + 1

Exercise: Create a course_title and a lesson_count variable. Increase the count by one and print both values.

lessons.title: Numbers and Calculations
lessons.content:
Explanation: Python can combine numbers with arithmetic operators. Parentheses make calculation order explicit, and division produces a floating-point result.

Example: completed = 3
total = 8
percentage = (completed / total) * 100
print(percentage)

Exercise: Calculate the total cost of three notebooks at 4.5 each. Explain why multiplying before adding matters when delivery costs 2.

lessons.title: Strings and Formatting
lessons.content:
Explanation: Strings store text. An f-string inserts expressions into a readable message without changing the original values.

Example: name = 'Mira'
lessons = 3
message = f'{name} completed {lessons} lessons.'
print(message)

Exercise: Build a sentence containing a course title and its module count using an f-string.

lessons.title: Boolean Decisions
lessons.content:
Explanation: Conditions evaluate to true or false. Use if, elif, and else to select one path; indentation defines the statements belonging to each branch.

Example: score = 72
if score >= 60:
    print('Ready for the next lesson')
else:
    print('Review and retry')

Exercise: Write a condition that prints 'Complete' when completed equals total and 'Keep learning' otherwise.

lessons.title: Lists and For Loops
lessons.content:
Explanation: A list groups values in order. A for loop visits each value, making repeated work clear without copying the same statement.

Example: topics = ['variables', 'conditions', 'loops']
for topic in topics:
    print(f'Review: {topic}')

Exercise: Create a list of three learning goals and print each goal on its own line.

lessons.title: While Loops and Boundaries
lessons.content:
Explanation: A while loop repeats while its condition remains true. Update the condition's inputs so the loop can stop, and check the boundary before starting.

Example: remaining = 3
while remaining > 0:
    print(remaining)
    remaining -= 1

Exercise: Write a countdown from five to one. Describe what happens if the decrement is removed.

lessons.title: Functions and Return Values
lessons.content:
Explanation: A function gives a task a name. Parameters provide inputs, while return makes a result available to the caller without requiring a printed message.

Example: def remaining_lessons(total, completed):
    return max(total - completed, 0)

remaining = remaining_lessons(8, 3)

Exercise: Write a function that returns the area of a rectangle and call it with two different inputs.

lessons.title: Dictionaries for Named Data
lessons.content:
Explanation: Dictionaries associate keys with values. They suit small records whose fields have distinct meanings; get can supply a default for an absent key.

Example: course = {'title': 'Python Fundamentals', 'lessons': 9}
print(course['title'])
print(course.get('category', 'General'))

Exercise: Create a learner dictionary containing a name and completed count. Update the count and read an optional nickname safely.

lessons.title: Handling Expected Errors
lessons.content:
Explanation: Some operations fail for ordinary input reasons. Catch the specific exception you can handle and let unrelated failures remain visible.

Example: raw_count = 'nine'
try:
    count = int(raw_count)
except ValueError:
    print('Enter a whole number')

Exercise: Ask for a number and handle invalid numeric text with ValueError. Explain why catching every exception would hide useful information.

courses.title: Modern React Development
courses.description: Build understandable React interfaces using components, state, forms, and deliberate data flow.

lessons.title: Components and JSX
Passing Props
Lists and Stable Keys
State and Event Handlers
Controlled Form Inputs
lessons.content:
Explanation: A controlled input reads its value from state and updates that state on change. A visible label makes the field understandable beyond its placeholder.

Example: const [title, setTitle] = useState('');
// Inside a component:
<label>Course title
  <input value={title} onChange={event => setTitle(event.target.value)} />
</label>

Exercise: Build a form with a controlled course-title input. Prevent submission when the trimmed value is empty.

lessons.title: Sharing State
Effects and Cleanup
Explicit Loading and Error States
Accessible Component Composition
lessons.content:
Explanation: Prefer native elements for familiar interactions. Buttons provide keyboard activation and disabled behavior, while meaningful text explains the action.

Example: <button type="button" disabled={isSaving} onClick={save}>
  {isSaving ? 'Saving...' : 'Save lesson'}
</button>

Exercise: Replace a clickable div with a native button. Check its accessible name and how it behaves when focused.

courses.title: UI/UX Design Essentials
courses.description: Practice task-focused interface design, clear hierarchy, accessible interactions, and small usability studies.

lessons.title: User Goals Before Screens
lessons.content:
Explanation: A useful interface starts with a task someone wants to complete. Separate the user's goal from a proposed control so you can evaluate several solutions.

Example: Goal: resume the next unfinished lesson.
Possible support: a clearly labeled Continue Learning action with course context.

Exercise: Write a goal for a first-time learner and another for an instructor. Avoid naming interface controls in the goals.

lessons.title: Simple Journey Mapping
lessons.content:
Explanation: A journey describes the steps between intent and outcome. Mark uncertainty and failure points instead of assuming every user follows the ideal path.

Example: Discover course -> inspect curriculum -> sign in -> enroll -> open lesson.
Potential interruption: the course becomes unpublished before enrollment.

Exercise: Map a learner's first course enrollment. Identify one place where clearer feedback would reduce uncertainty.

lessons.title: Content Hierarchy
lessons.content:
Explanation: Hierarchy helps people decide what to read first. Use meaningful headings, grouping, and concise copy before adding decorative emphasis.

Example: Course page order: title and purpose, learning level, curriculum, enrollment action, supporting details.

Exercise: Arrange five pieces of course information in reading order and explain the first two choices.

lessons.title: Spacing and Alignment
lessons.content:
Explanation: Consistent spacing communicates relationships. Nearby items appear related, while larger gaps separate groups; alignment gives the page a predictable reading path.

Example: Use 8px between a label and hint, 16px between fields, and 32px between form groups as a starting scale.

Exercise: Inspect a form sketch. Mark which gaps communicate a group and which separate independent tasks.

lessons.title: Color and Contrast
lessons.content:
Explanation: Color can support meaning, but it cannot carry meaning alone. Check foreground/background contrast and pair status colors with text or recognizable symbols.

Example: An invalid field has a clear error message and an error border, rather than a red border by itself.

Exercise: Design a completion badge that remains understandable in grayscale. Identify its text and background contrast pair.

lessons.title: Clear Interactive States
lessons.content:
Explanation: Controls should communicate what can be done and what is happening. Include default, hover, focus, disabled, loading, and error behavior where relevant.

Example: A Save button changes to Saving..., prevents repeated submission, and announces a failure without discarding the entered title.

Exercise: Describe the states of an enrollment button before, during, and after a failed request.

lessons.title: Low-Fidelity Wireframes
lessons.content:
Explanation: A wireframe explores structure without making visual polish the main discussion. Show real labels and plausible content lengths to uncover layout problems early.

Example: Sketch a course editor with a heading, metadata form, curriculum list, and save action using simple rectangles and text.

Exercise: Draw two different layouts for the same course-detail task and note the trade-off of each.

lessons.title: Small Usability Sessions
lessons.content:
Explanation: Ask participants to perform a realistic task without explaining the solution. Observe decisions and hesitation, then distinguish observations from your interpretation.

Example: Task: find a beginner course and locate its lesson list.
Observation: the participant opened three cards before finding the curriculum label.

Exercise: Write one neutral task prompt and three observations you would record without guessing the participant's thoughts.

lessons.title: Prioritizing Design Changes
lessons.content:
Explanation: Prioritize problems by task impact and supporting evidence. A confusing primary action usually deserves attention before a decorative inconsistency.

Example: Issue A: enrollment failure has no recovery action.
Issue B: two decorative icons differ slightly in size.
Fix A first because it blocks task completion.

Exercise: Choose one usability issue, propose the smallest correction, and define how you would check whether it helped.

courses.title: SQL & PostgreSQL
courses.description: Query relational data, understand keys and joins, and practice safe changes with PostgreSQL transactions.

lessons.title: Rows, Columns, and Types
lessons.content:
Explanation: A relational table stores records as rows with named, typed columns. Choose types that describe the values rather than storing every value as arbitrary text.

Example: A lessons table might contain id UUID, title TEXT, position INTEGER, and created_at TIMESTAMPTZ.

Exercise: Define suitable column types for a course title, lesson position, and publication date.

lessons.title: Selecting and Filtering
lessons.content:
Explanation: SELECT chooses columns, while WHERE restricts the returned rows. Explicit column names keep a query's output easier to understand.

Example: SELECT title, level
FROM courses
WHERE status = 'published' AND level = 'beginner';

Exercise: Write a query returning published course titles in the Design category.

lessons.title: Ordering and Limiting
lessons.content:
Explanation: ORDER BY makes result order intentional. Add a unique tie-breaker when values can match, particularly when a page displays only part of the result.

Example: SELECT id, title
FROM courses
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id ASC
LIMIT 9;

Exercise: Explain why ordering only by a shared creation timestamp can make pagination unstable.

lessons.title: Primary and Foreign Keys
lessons.content:
Explanation: A primary key identifies a row. A foreign key requires a reference to an existing parent and helps prevent disconnected records.

Example: modules.course_id references courses.id.
A module cannot refer to a course ID that does not exist.

Exercise: Draw the course-to-module-to-lesson relationships. Identify the foreign key on each child table.

lessons.title: Joining Related Data
lessons.content:
Explanation: A join combines rows using a relationship. Think about whether you need only matching rows or also parents without children.

Example: SELECT c.title, m.title AS module_title
FROM courses AS c
JOIN modules AS m ON m.course_id = c.id;

Exercise: Describe how a LEFT JOIN differs when a course has no modules.

lessons.title: Grouping and Counting
lessons.content:
Explanation: Aggregate functions summarize records. GROUP BY defines the groups; count the child key when a left join should include zero-child parents.

Example: SELECT c.id, c.title, COUNT(m.id) AS module_count
FROM courses AS c
LEFT JOIN modules AS m ON m.course_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.title;

Exercise: Write a query counting lessons per module, including modules with no lessons.

lessons.title: Inserts and Constraints
lessons.content:
Explanation: Constraints protect data even when several clients write concurrently. A unique slug constraint is stronger than an application-only duplicate check.

Example: INSERT INTO courses (id, instructor_id, title, slug, level, status)
VALUES (:id, :instructor_id, 'Data Basics', 'data-basics', 'beginner', 'draft');
The placeholders must be bound by the database client.

Exercise: Identify the constraint needed to prevent two modules sharing one position within a course.

lessons.title: Transactions and Rollback
lessons.content:
Explanation: A transaction groups related changes into a unit. Commit when the complete operation is valid; roll back when any part fails.

Example: BEGIN;
-- Insert a course and its curriculum.
-- If validation fails, issue ROLLBACK instead of COMMIT.

Exercise: Describe why inserting a module and its lessons in one transaction is safer than committing each incomplete step.

lessons.title: Indexes and Query Plans

courses.title: FastAPI Backend Development
courses.description: Build small validated APIs with clear responsibilities, database sessions, and server-enforced access rules.

lessons.title: Routes and HTTP Methods
Request Schemas
lessons.content:
Explanation: A request model describes acceptable input. Validation rejects malformed data before the operation reaches persistence, but business rules still belong in the service.

Example: from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class CourseInput(BaseModel):
    title: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=200)

Exercise: Add a level field restricted to beginner, intermediate, or advanced. Decide where a duplicate-slug rule should be checked.

lessons.title: Response Schemas
Request-Scoped Sessions
lessons.content:
Explanation: A session coordinates database work for an operation. Create it for the request, release it reliably, and keep transaction ownership explicit.

Example: def get_db():
    with SessionFactory() as session:
        yield session

# A route can receive it with Depends(get_db).

Exercise: Explain why a single mutable session should not be shared by all simultaneous requests.

lessons.title: Service and Repository Responsibilities
lessons.content:
Explanation: Routes translate HTTP concerns, services enforce business rules, and repositories express database queries. Introduce each layer when it has a clear responsibility.

Example: Route: validate a course ID.
Service: verify ownership and publication rules.
Repository: load the course with its modules.

Exercise: Place duplicate-slug handling, a SELECT query, and an HTTP response schema in their appropriate responsibilities.

lessons.title: Atomic Writes
lessons.content:
Explanation: A multi-record operation should not leave an invalid partial result. Flush can surface database constraints without making a change permanent; commit completes the transaction.

Example: try:
    session.add(course)
    session.flush()
    # Validate the complete curriculum.
    session.commit()
except Exception:
    session.rollback()
    raise

Exercise: Describe what should remain in the database if the second lesson insert fails during course creation.

lessons.title: Authentication and Authorization
lessons.content:
Explanation: Authentication identifies the caller; authorization decides whether that caller may perform the action. Check current roles and ownership on the server.

Example: A valid token can identify an instructor, but editing course B must still require ownership of course B or explicit administrator permission.

Exercise: Explain why hiding an Edit button is not sufficient to secure a course-update endpoint.

lessons.title: Useful Error Responses
lessons.content:
Explanation: Status codes communicate the outcome consistently. Return safe, actionable messages without exposing SQL text, credentials, or internal stack traces.

Example: Use 404 for an unavailable course, 403 for a forbidden action, 409 for a slug conflict, and 422 for invalid request data.

Exercise: Write a duplicate-slug error message that helps an instructor recover without exposing database details.

lessons.title: Focused API Tests
lessons.content:
Explanation: Test observable behavior through the request boundary and isolate persistence from valuable data. Include rejected requests, not just successful ones.

Example: from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
client = TestClient(app)
response = client.get('/health')
assert response.status_code == 200
assert response.json() == {'status': 'ok'}

Exercise: Design one success test and one ownership-rejection test for updating a draft course.

courses.title: JavaScript Essentials
courses.description: Understand JavaScript values, functions, collections, and browser events through small practical tasks.

lessons.title: Values and Bindings
Conditions and Equality
Functions and Parameters
Arrays and Transformations
Objects and Optional Data
DOM Events

courses.title: Git & GitHub Workflow
courses.description: Practice small local commits, focused branches, and readable reviews without destructive history shortcuts.

lessons.title: Inspecting Your Working Tree
lessons.content:
Explanation: Git distinguishes edits, staged changes, and committed history. Inspect the current state before deciding which files belong in a change.

Example: git status --short
git diff
# These commands inspect local changes without publishing them.

Exercise: Describe the difference between an unstaged modification and a staged modification.

lessons.title: Focused Commits
lessons.content:
Explanation: A commit records the staged snapshot. Stage specific files and review that snapshot so unrelated edits and secrets do not enter the change.

Example: git add README.md
git diff --cached
# After reviewing the snapshot, create a concise commit when authorized.

Exercise: Write a commit message for correcting a lesson title. Explain why reviewing the staged diff matters.

lessons.title: Branches for a Single Task
lessons.content:
Explanation: A branch names a line of work. Keep one task focused so review and integration stay understandable.

Example: git switch -c feat/course-search
# Work on one change, then inspect git status and git diff.

Exercise: Propose a branch name for an enrollment error-message fix and list two unrelated changes that should stay out.

lessons.title: Reading a Diff
lessons.content:
Explanation: A diff shows how a proposal changes behavior. Review the result as well as individual lines, including tests and documentation.

Example: git diff --stat
git diff -- README.md
# The first command summarizes scope; the second inspects one file.

Exercise: Review a small local diff and identify its purpose, evidence, and any unrelated edits.

lessons.title: Resolving Conflicts Deliberately
lessons.content:
Explanation: A conflict means Git could not combine competing edits automatically. Understand both intentions before choosing the final content; never accept a side blindly.

Example: Conflict markers separate the competing versions. Read both, edit the desired combined result, remove the markers, and review the complete file.

Exercise: Describe how you would resolve two changes to the same lesson title without losing an intentional correction.

lessons.title: Preparing a Review
lessons.content:
Explanation: A useful review explains the problem, resulting behavior, and validation. Check repository policy before publishing a branch or opening a pull request.

Example: Review note: Course search now preserves category filters. Validation: focused filter tests pass. Limitation: live API testing is pending.

Exercise: Draft a short review description for a course-form fix, including an honest statement of what was tested.

courses.title: Web Development Foundations
courses.description: Connect semantic HTML, responsive CSS, and browser-server communication to build understandable web pages.

lessons.title: Semantic HTML
lessons.content:
Explanation: HTML elements communicate the structure and purpose of content. Prefer headings, landmarks, links, and buttons over generic containers for meaningful tasks. Example:

Learning journal

This week's goals

Complete one lesson and write a reflection.

Exercise: Outline a course page with one main heading, a curriculum section, and a link to another page.

lessons.title: The CSS Box Model
Responsive Layouts
Accessible Forms
lessons.content:
Explanation: A form needs understandable labels, useful validation, and predictable submission. Placeholder text is a hint rather than a replacement for a label.

Example: <label for="course-title">Course title</label>
<input id="course-title" name="title" required maxlength="200">
<button type="submit">Save course</button>

Exercise: Add a hint associated with an input using aria-describedby and explain when an error message should appear.

lessons.title: Browser and Server Requests
Inspecting a Page
lessons.content:
Explanation: Developer tools help separate markup, styling, and network problems. Inspect evidence before changing code, and test keyboard use as well as pointer use.

Example: For an overflowing card: inspect its computed width, check its parent's layout, then inspect any long unbroken text before choosing a correction.

Exercise: Inspect a page at a narrow width, navigate its controls using Tab, and record one concrete improvement.
